newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Fuel crisis may shut Chernobyl soon, official says.
newsitem.headline: Fuel crisis may shut Chernobyl soon, official says.

text.p: Ukraine's Chernobyl nuclear power plant, owed millions of dollars and running low on fuel, has halved output and may have to shut down in a month -- a step which could hit safety levels, a spokesman said on Thursday.

"Late last night the working capacity of the third reactor was reduced by 50 percent. The station lacks fuel. We can operate for one month with what we have left," the plant's chief spokesman, Valery Idelson, told Reuters.
"If there is no fuel we will stop the reactor. We have never been in a situation like this before," he added.
Lack of fuel forced the plant to reduce output by 20 percent last year but that was the biggest reduction since the station's reactor number four blew up in April 1986.
Idelson said shutting down the reactor could affect safety levels as power was needed to maintain and warm that and another reactor, number one, which have not been fully de-commissioned.
"Okay, we'll get the electricity from the grid, but God help us if something happens -- like a storm or tornado -- and the station gets cut off," Idelson said.
"Our autonomous diesel engine is not powerful and can work only for very short periods of time," he added.
Idelson said consumers owed Chernobyl more than 200 million hryvnias ($110 million) and the station had no money to buy more nuclear fuel from Russia.
Ukraine's five nuclear plants, which supply 45 percent of its electricity, are owed 1.53 billion hryvnias ($850 million).
Deputy Energy Minister Valentyn Bondarenko told a news conference separately that 13,000 industrial consumers and 10,000 others had been cut off from the grid for non-payment.
Energy ministry data issued last month said the sector's thermal, nuclear and hydro-electric plants were owed more than two billion dollars.
Chernobyl has been operating on fuel obtained in return for Ukraine giving up nuclear warheads to Russia under a 1994 deal signed by Kiev, Moscow and Washington.
The station owes Russian producers $3.5 million and the last fuel delivery was shipped to the station last July.
Viktor Chebrov, head of the Derzhkomatom state nuclear authority, said last month Russia would make its last delivery of nuclear fuel as compensation for warheads this year.
He also said Kiev should pay $167 million to Russian producers by the end of the year for "non-compensatory" fuel.
Western countries have pledged $3.1 billion in credits and aid to enable Ukraine to meet President Leonid Kuchma's promise to close the station by the year 2000.
But Kiev says it may revise the decision if the West, and the Group of Seven leading industrial nations in particular, do not come up in time with all the promised funds.

Reactor No.4 caught fire and exploded in 1986, sending clouds of radiation across Europe, while the second reactor was stopped in 1991 after a small fire and the first switched off last November in line with the closure programme.
Idelson said the mood of Chernobyl's 5,000 workers was gloomy because of salary delays, the impending closure of the plant and unclear prospects for their professional futures.
"To say the atmosphere is far from happy is putting it mildly. It's a kind of mild depression," he said.
